title: LCIA Challenge Decision — Decision 2 (09/01/2018)
text:
DECISION RENDERED ON 9 JANUARY 2018
Subject: The Claimant filed two challenges to the Sole Arbitrator (selected by the LCIA
Court) pursuant to Articles 10.1(iii), 10.2(i), 10.2(ii) and 10.3 of the LCIA Rules
2014.
Outcome: Rejected
Seat: London, England
Governing Law of English law
the Contract:
Summary: The first challenge related to certain procedural decisions issued by the Sole
Arbitrator in connection with a security for costs application made by the
Respondent.
The Claimant argued that the Sole Arbitrator: (i) made the procedural
decisions without having heard from the Claimant; (ii) acted partially in the
Respondents’ favour; (iii) imposed an “extremely short timeframe” and
“unprecedented cash flow burdens” for providing security; and (iv) acted in
breach of nemo iudex in causa sua when ruling that the Sole Arbitrator’s
previous ruling “was not premature” and that the Sole Arbitrator would
continue to apply a “threshold test” to determine whether to allow an
application for reconsideration.
The second challenge related to the application of a “threshold test” by the
Sole Arbitrator in relation to the Claimant’s application to set aside a decision
on security for costs. The Claimant argued that: (i) the application of the
“threshold test” was unfair since the Claimant was “not heard” on the test; (ii)
the Sole Arbitrator acted unfairly by proceeding to assess whether the
“threshold test” had been met and by weighing the evidence on the merits
without having heard from the Claimant regarding how the evidence ought to
be assessed and weighed; and (iii) the Sole Arbitrator reached an “entirely
contrary conclusion” on the Claimant’s ability to meet an adverse cost order
when compared to the Sole Arbitrator’s findings in a previous decision.
The LCIA Court addressed both challenges in a single decision and rejected
both challenges.
Challenges brought against arbitrators for their alleged failure to adopt
suitable procedures “should only be available where the conduct of the
arbitrator is such as to go so beyond anything that could reasonably be
defended that substantial injustice has resulted or will result. The provision is

not intended to allow the Court to substitute its own view as to how the arbitral
proceedings should be conducted.” (The Petrol Ranger).
The Sole Arbitrator has the “widest discretion” to discharge general duties,
which include the duty to act fairly and impartially, to give each disputing side
the opportunity of putting its case, to adopt procedures suitable to the
circumstances of the arbitration and conduct the proceedings in a fair,
efficient and expeditious manner.
An allegation that an arbitrator acted unfairly because of flouting the right of
putting one’s case must be assessed in light of all relevant circumstances,
including the other general duties of the arbitrator to conduct the arbitration
efficiently as well as the conduct of the parties during the proceedings.
The refusal to stay the proceedings pending the resolution of the security
issue, as well as the refusal to bifurcate the proceedings are procedural rulings
that fall within the undisputed discretionary power of the Sole Arbitrator.
The LCIA Court reviewed the decisions and the procedural steps leading to
them and concluded that the Claimant was not deprived of the right of putting
its case, and that the Sole Arbitrator did not act unfairly or partially and did
not fail to adopt suitable procedures.
Regarding the “threshold test”, the Claimant was made fully aware by the Sole
Arbitrator that an application for reconsideration needed to spell out “a
justifiable basis” if it was to be entertained. Thus, the Claimant knew in
advance that the Sole Arbitrator would apply a so-called “threshold test”, and
therefore had the opportunity either to provide such “basis” or else to argue
against the application of such “threshold test” by providing relevant
submissions and authorities. It chose not to do so.

Preamble
1. This Decision of […] the LCIA Court arises out of two challenges (the “Challenges”) brought by the
Claimant in an LCIA arbitration against the Sole Arbitrator of the Tribunal […] (the “Sole Arbitrator”).
2. In the first challenge of 22 September 2017 (the “First Challenge”), the Claimant challenges the
appointment of [the Sole Arbitrator] on the ground that circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable
doubts as to [the Sole Arbitrator’s] impartiality or independence. By reference to three decisions dated
9, 13 and 19 September 2017 respectively, the Claimant argues that the Sole Arbitrator: (i) failed to
act fairly and impartially, (ii) failed to give Claimant any, still less reasonable, opportunity of putting its
case and dealing with Respondents’, (iii) failed to adopt suitable procedures, and (iv) acted in
deliberate violation of the agreement to arbitrate.
3. In the second challenge of 3 November 2017 (the “Second Challenge”), the Claimant refers to the
decision of 20 October 2017 to argue that the Sole Arbitrator: (i) failed to act fairly and impartially, (ii)
failed to give Claimant any, still less reasonable, opportunity of putting its case and dealing with
Respondents’, (iii) failed to adopt suitable procedures, and (iv) acted in deliberate violation of the
agreement to arbitrate.

C. Procedural History
10. The following does not constitute a full procedural history of this challenge proceeding and even less
of the arbitration, as that is not necessary to deal with the current Challenges, but is limited to those

Challenges are set out in full.
1) Procedural History of the Arbitration
11. On 24 January 2017, the Claimant filed its Request for Arbitration, dated 19 January 2017.
12. On 8 March 2017, the First Respondent filed a Response to the Request for Arbitration.
13. On 15 March 2017, the LCIA Court confirmed the appointment of [the] Sole Arbitrator.
14. On 17 March 2017, the Sole Arbitrator set out a calendar for the first procedural steps, including for
the filing of the Claimant’s Statement of Case, the Respondents’ Statement of Defence and the
Claimant’s Statement of Reply. He further informed the Parties that he considered holding a case
management conference (“CMC”) shortly after the Statement of Reply.
15. On 5 May 2017, the Claimant served its Statement of Case.
16. On 9 May 2017, the Sole Arbitrator extended the filing of the Respondents’ Statement of Defence until
3 July 2017.1 He further informed the Parties of his decision to hold a CMC in person and before the
second round of written exchanges.
17. On 30 May 2017, after having consulted the Parties, the Sole Arbitrator informed the Parties that the
CMC would take place on 20 July 2017.2
18. On 3 July 2017, the Respondents filed their Statement of Defence, which included in its Part IV an
application for security for costs.
19. On 5 July 2017, the Sole Arbitrator informed the Parties that he expected to hear at the CMC oral
submissions inter alia on the Respondents’ application for security for costs.3 He therefore instructed

the Respondents’ application for security for costs.

20. On 6 July 2017, the Respondents requested that the Sole Arbitrator refrain from deciding the

21. On the same day, the Sole Arbitrator requested that the Respondents confirm that their request did
not extend to the Respondents’ application for security for costs. Having received the Respondents’

22. On 7 July 2017, the Claimant informed the Sole Arbitrator that the Respondents’ application “could

23. On 10 July 2017, the Sole Arbitrator wrote to the Parties providing directions on the CMC. In relation

“Respondents’ Application for security for costs
This application will be heard on 20 July 2017.
The Respondents have made the application at Part IV of their Statement of Defence. The submissions
in support of the application are at paragraphs 93-95, and documents in support are exhibited at
Annex C and D.
The Claimant is directed to serve any submissions and documentary evidence on which it wishes to

The Respondents may serve any reply submissions by close of business on Tuesday 18 July 2017. Both

In the first instance, I will decide on or after 20 July whether security should be granted. If I decide
that the Claimant should provide security, then I will deal subsequently with the amount and form of
that security and may request further submissions in writing in that regard to be provided following
the 20 July hearing”.8
24. On 12 July 2017, the Claimant filed a letter addressing certain concerns regarding the Sole Arbitrator’s
directions of 10 July 2017 on the Respondent’s application for security for costs in the following terms:
“Dear Sir,

Decision 2 - 10

Thank you for your email of 10 July 2017 regarding directions for the forthcoming hearing. Without
prejudice to the submissions we have been ordered to make on Friday, 14th, with respect we have
some misgivings concerning the manner in which you plan to deal with the Respondent’s application
for security for costs, which we feel obliged to ventilate forthwith to afford you an opportunity to
consider the Claimant’s concerns and perhaps modify your directions.
It seems to us that your Directions as they stand now bifurcate the procedure for the application and
give rise to an opportunity for the Respondents to add in new evidence and/or make further
submissions, thus providing an opportunity to rescue an otherwise failing submission.
Moreover, the proposed additional procedure as set out in your Directions then requires the Claimant
to review its evidence and perhaps add to its evidence in response and make further submissions after
20 July in response to the Respondents’ further submissions. This is a disproportionately costly and
unnecessary approach to an application for security for costs. Such applications are reasonably
straightforward and the grounds and evidential requirements are well established.
If, as the Claimant submits, the Respondents’ application for security for costs is insufficiently
evidenced or motivated for it to succeed on 20 July, then it should fail, and that should be an end of
the matter.
The Claimant’s position is that the Respondents are not entitled to any second chance to make good
a defective application and that their application should stand or fall on the basis of the evidence
adduced and referred to in their application forming part of their Defence. You have directed that the
Respondents’ case is at Part IV and Annexures C and D of their Defence. That is their entire application,
and that is all that the Claimant should be required to deal with, on 20 July or subsequently apart from
any answer to the submissions the Claimant files on 14 July which you have directed to be served on
18 July.
In the circumstances, and respectfully, the Claimant invites you to reconsider your directions so that
the matter is concluded on 20 July on the basis of the application which is now before you.
Meanwhile the Claimant reserves its position.
Yours sincerely
[…]
[The Claimant]”.9

26. On 15 July 2017, the Sole Arbitrator acknowledged receipt, inter alia, of the Claimant’s witness
statement in support of the Claimant’s opposition to the Respondents’ application for security for
costs. The Sole Arbitrator further stated the following in relevant part:
“I have not yet received the Claimant’s submissions on the security for costs application […] which
[was] due yesterday. If these have been sent but not received by me, please let me know”.11
27. On 17 July 2017, the Claimant informed the Sole Arbitrator that it was ascertaining “what has
occurred” and that it would revert “as soon as possible”, further offering “sincere apologies for any
inconvenience”.12 On the same day, the Claimant offered “profuse apologies at the additional delay in
filing submissions”, further stating that such submissions would be filed the next day.13
28. On the same day, the Sole Arbitrator informed the Parties that he would give further directions “once
the Claimant’s submissions have been served tomorrow morning”. He further requested that the
Claimant “explain the cause of the delay that has occurred when serving those submissions”.14
29. On 18 July 2017, at 12:05, the Claimant filed an email […] purportedly showing that “the Claimant is
now fully compliant and no longer in penalty”.15 At 13:10, the Sole Arbitrator acknowledged receipt
of the Claimant’s email, while at the same time informing the Parties in the following terms that the
Claimant had still not filed its submissions on the Respondent’s application for security for costs or the
reasons for the delay:
“Dear [all]
I have just received [the] email below, attaching an email from [X].
As you are aware, the Claimant was due to file submissions in respect of the Respondents’ application
for security for costs by last Friday. […] In my email to the parties of Saturday 15 July, I noted that
these submissions and proposed directions had not been filed. Yesterday, in response, [Y]’s first email
said that he was looking into matters and then, in an email received by me at 17:38 apologised and
said that the Claimant’s submissions would be filed this morning. The Respondents send an email
putting on record the difficulties the delay placed upon them, given that they are due to file reply
submissions on the security for costs application by the end of today.
I directed in my email of yesterday evening that when the Claimant served its submissions this
morning, it should explain the cause of the delay that has occurred.
It is now after 1pm and the email that I have just received from [Y] does not provide the Claimant’s
submissions, does not set out the Claimant’s proposed directions and does not explain why the delay
has arisen. The Claimant’s continuing and repeated failure to comply with the Tribunal’s directions is
jeopardizing the fair conduct of Thursday’s hearing.

“Dear [Sole Arbitrator],

39. On 24 August 2017, the Sole Arbitrator invited the Respondents to comment on the contents of [B’s]

40. On 25 August 2017, the Claimant requested an extension until 15 September 2017 to file submissions

41. On 27 August 2017, the Sole Arbitrator responded in the following terms to the Claimant’s letter of 25
August 2017:
Security for Costs submissions
In its letter of 25 August, [B] state that it is ‘currently envisaged’ that the Claimant will make a request
that my decision to award security for costs of 31 July 2017 (‘the Decision’) be ‘reconsidered, set-aside,
discharged or varied’. It is suggested that such a request should be made with the submissions on the
quantum and form of the security to be granted which are currently due from the Claimant on 28
August 2017. The Claimant has requested an extension of time to 15 September to make its
submissions.
The Claimant has not explained on what basis the Decision should be revisited. Unless and until I am
persuaded that there is a justifiable basis for reviewing the Decision, I do not consider that it is
appropriate to suspend the operation of that Decision. As the Respondents have submitted, the
submissions on the form and quantum of the security to be provided concern discrete and
straightforward issues. I consider that the Claimant can be expected to address those issues with
assistance from [B]. Accordingly, the Claimant is granted an extension of time to Friday 1 September
2017 to file the submissions due under paragraph 15 of the Decision.
If the Claimant decides that it does intend to seek to set-aside, discharge or vary the Decision, then it
should set out the basis on which it considers this to be justified. I will then consider, after taking into
account the views of the Respondents, whether it is appropriate to entertain any such application.27
42. On 1 September 2017, the Claimant filed its submissions on amount and form of security for costs, as

circumstances, where [the Claimant’s] new solicitors ([B]) have just been instructed and new counsel

revocation of an arbitrator’s appointment in LCIA proceedings. It follows from Article 10.1 and 10.2

157. With respect to bias, Article 10.1 of the LCIA Rules provides that an arbitrator may be challenged “if
circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to that arbitrator’s impartiality or
independence”. It is generally accepted in international arbitration that the notion of impartiality
refers to the absence of bias or predisposition towards a party, whereas the notion of independence
refers to the absence of external control.
158. The Parties agree that the relevant test is not actual bias, but apparent bias. As was stated by Lord
Hope in Millar v Dickinson, “the appearance of independence and impartiality is just as important as
the question whether these qualities exist in fact. Justice must not only be done, it must be seen to be
done”.139

“whether the fair-minded and informed observer, having considered the facts, would conclude that
there is a real possibility that an arbitrator is partial to a party”.140 The test was articulated in the
following terms in Laker Airways v FLS Aerospace Ltd:
“The test is an objective one – whether circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to an
arbitrator’s impartiality. The test is thus objective in at least two respects: the court must find that

justify doubts as to impartiality. An unjustifiable or perhaps unreasonable doubt is not sufficient: it is
not enough honestly to say that one lost confidence in the arbitrator’s impartiality. On the other hand,
doubts, if justifiable, are sufficient: it is not necessary to prove actual bias”.141

against them, and has the opportunity to put forward that party's own case”.143

the fairness in the conduct of the arbitration. However, an allegation that an arbitrator acted unfairly
because of flouting the right of putting one’s case must be assessed in the light of all relevant
circumstances, including the other general duties of the arbitrator to conduct the arbitration
efficiently as well as the conduct of the parties during the proceedings. As was held in The Petrol
Ranger, challenges brought against arbitrators for their alleged failure to adopt suitable procedures
“should only be available where the conduct of the arbitrator is such as to go so beyond anything that
could reasonably be defended that substantial injustice has resulted or will result. The provision is not
intended to allow the Court to substitute its own view as to how the arbitral proceedings should be
conducted”.144

the following: “To the extent necessary, this is a material change”.164 Similarly, the Claimant argued

provided its views on the application of the so-called Threshold Test, by arguing that, in its view, it had
provided the necessary evidence constituting a material change allowing reconsidering the previous

210. Similarly, in its Reply, the Claimant argued on the applicability and application of the so-called
Threshold Test.166 Referring to Orb v Ruhan and taking issue with the Respondents’ interpretation of
that decision, the Claimant argued that a lack of appeal in international arbitration should lead to the
possibility of “a review by the Tribunal itself, irrespective of material change”. The Claimant further
argued that only awards, not procedural decisions, are final, thus militating in favor of a “right to ask

provided its views yet again on the applicability of the so-called Threshold Test.
211. The Claimant further again argued that the evidence filed in support of its application constituted a
material change: “The availability of the financial statements is a material change”.168

opportunity to be heard on the application of the so-called Threshold Test and used it. This limb of the

evidence it adduced to its application. In fact, the Claimant did so when it argued that:

224. The Respondents request that the LCIA Court dismiss the Challenges “with an order for costs on an

225. Article 10.7 of the LCIA Rules provides in relevant part:
The LCIA Court may also determine whether, in what amount and to whom any party should pay
forthwith the costs of the challenge; and the LCIA Court may also refer all or any part of such costs to
the later decision of the Arbitral Tribunal and/or the LCIA Court under Article 28.
226. I have not received any costs submissions by the Parties. In these circumstances, I prefer to refer any
decision on the costs of the Challenges to a later decision of the Sole Arbitrator or the LCIA Court.
